title: Contoso Ltd. — Migrating an e-commerce app to Azure
scenario: Contoso is migrating an on-premises e-commerce application to Azure. The application has a web tier of IIS servers and a SQL Server database. Product images are uploaded by customers, are accessed frequently for the first 30 days, and are then rarely accessed.
context: The web tier must remain available during planned OS updates.
The database tier must survive a single datacenter failure.
Customer-uploaded images older than 30 days must automatically move to the cheapest storage.
Administrators must be able to securely manage the VMs without exposing RDP/SSH to the public internet.

questions.domain: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources
questions.prompt: What should you use to keep the web tier available during planned OS updates?
options: Place the VMs in an availability set
Place the VMs in a single fault domain
Add an NSG rule allowing update traffic
Deploy an ExpressRoute circuit
questions.explanation: An availability set spreads VMs across update domains, so planned maintenance/reboots affect only one update domain at a time.

questions.prompt: How should Contoso automatically move images older than 30 days to the cheapest storage?
options: Use a blob lifecycle management policy to transition to Cool, then Archive
Store all images in the Hot tier indefinitely
Manually copy blobs to a second storage account
Use Azure Files snapshots
questions.explanation: A lifecycle management policy automatically transitions blobs between tiers (e.g., Hot → Cool → Archive) based on age, minimizing cost.

questions.prompt: How should administrators securely access the VMs for management?
options: Connect through Azure Bastion
Allow RDP (3389) to the public internet in the NSG
Assign a public IP to every VM
Use VNet peering to the on-premises network
questions.explanation: Azure Bastion provides secure, browser-based RDP/SSH to VMs without exposing them to the public internet.

title: Adventure Works — Governance and identity at scale
scenario: Adventure Works has separate subscriptions for Development and Production. Multiple teams deploy resources into Development. The finance team requires every new resource to carry a cost-center tag, and auditors need read-only visibility into all resources.
context: Enforce a cost-center tag on every new resource.
Prevent the Development team from deploying resources into the Production subscription.
Grant auditors read-only access to all resources in Production.

questions.prompt: How should you enforce the cost-center tag on new resources?
options: Create and assign an Azure Policy that requires the tag
Create a resource lock on each resource
Assign the Contributor role to the finance team
Add the tag to the subscription display name
questions.explanation: An Azure Policy (e.g., 'require a tag on resources') enforces tagging and reports compliance.

questions.prompt: How should you prevent the Development team from deploying resources into the Production subscription?
options: Grant the Development team the Contributor role only on the Development subscription
Grant the Development team the Owner role on Production
Grant Contributor on both subscriptions
Delete the Production subscription
questions.explanation: RBAC is additive (no deny). By granting Contributor only at the Development subscription scope, the team cannot act in Production. There is no assignment that grants Production access.

questions.prompt: How should you grant auditors read-only access to all resources in the Production subscription?
options: Assign the Reader role at the Production subscription scope
Assign the Reader role to each resource group individually
Assign the Contributor role at the subscription scope
Add auditors to the Owners group
questions.explanation: Assigning the Reader role at the subscription scope provides read-only access to everything within it (and is inherited by all child scopes).
